How the sand is simulated

The sand is made of about 10,000–14,000 small clumps (6 mm) that collide, rub and roll against each other, the club and the ball. Every contact is worked out in steps of 10 microseconds through the whole strike. This is the discrete element method (Cundall & Strack 1979), the standard way to simulate granular materials. Golf researchers have used it for exactly this: Koizumi, Tsujiuchi, Horii et al. (2005) simulated bunker shots with a club head, a ball and sand particles, and matched high-speed film of real shots.

The sand

  • Contacts. Two clumps push apart like Hertzian spheres: stiff when pressed hard, soft at a touch. Sound therefore travels slowly near the surface, as in real loose sand. Tsuji damping makes collisions very lossy (restitution about 0.3). Sideways, a contact acts like a spring until it slips at Coulomb friction (Cundall–Strack, Luding 2008).
  • Angularity. Real bunker sand is angular, so grains don't roll freely. Rolling resistance stands in for that (Ai et al. 2011). Friction and rolling resistance were tuned together with a lifted-cylinder test, the usual way DEM sands are calibrated. The piles stand at the angles of repose measured for bunker sands, about 30° (fine, rounded), 33° (medium) and 35° (coarse, angular), from the USGA bunker-sand studies.
  • Water. Damp sand sticks together through tiny water bridges between grains (Herminghaus 2005). The bridge force is 2πRγ for a real grain, scaled to the clump size so the bed is just as cohesive. Cohesion switches on with the first bit of water and stays nearly the same over a wide range of wetness (Scheel et al. 2008). It disappears as the pores fill. Soaked sand is heavier and draggy instead.
  • Hardness. A bunker that hasn't been raked gets trodden, rained on and crusted. Its grains are lightly cemented. This uses the bonded-particle model (Potyondy & Cundall 2004): bonds hold until the club or ball breaks them, and broken bonds stay broken.
  • Depth. The sand sits on a firm base. With only 2–3 cm of sand, the club meets the base.

The club

  • Sole and bounce. A sand wedge's sole is curved front to back and heel to toe, so it meets the sand at one point and the contact grows. The bounce angle sets how round it is.
  • Swing path. You choose where the leading edge enters (Titleist's advice: 3½–4 inches behind the ball) and how deep the cut is planned to go. That fixes the arc and the angle of attack.
  • What the sand does. The arms hold the head on its arc (stiff along the shaft) and keep driving it. The sand pushes back, lifting the head (bounce) and slowing it, so the actual cut is shallower than planned.

The ball

  • In a proper splash shot the face never touches the ball: a cushion of sand pushes it out. The sand trapped between the face and the ball is only a few real grains thick, too thin for 6 mm clumps. So that layer is modelled as sheared granular friction (GDR MiDi 2004). The ball's spin comes from it: less sand between face and ball, more spin. That matches what TrackMan bunker testing shows.
  • From launch, the ball flies on the game's flight model.

How it compares with real shots

  • Launch. At 20 m/s (45 mph) club speed with a 56° wedge entering 9 cm behind the ball, it launches at about 12–13 m/s and 35–40°, with about 3,000 rpm. That's roughly what TrackMan bunker tests show. McPhee needed about 28–30 m/s club speed to carry 18 m.
  • Club speed. The club loses about a quarter of its speed in the sand.
  • Entry and depth. Further behind or deeper means less ball speed and less spin. A field study found correlations of −0.98 between carry and entry distance and −0.91 between carry and cut depth (Wivoul et al., ISBS).
  • Landing balls. How deep a dropped ball goes grows steadily with impact speed, as in granular impact experiments (Katsuragi & Durian 2007; Goldman & Umbanhowar 2008). Fast, steep landings in soft, fine sand make fried eggs.

Untidy bunkers and blame

Tidiness adds the footprints and splash craters players left without raking. Each one is a 24-byte record: type, position, heading, size, depth, a seed for the detail, who left it, when, and whether it was put right. The dent is rebuilt procedurally from the record, so every device draws the same bunker, and the multiplayer game can show who to blame. Rake it marks them repaired.

What's simplified

The clumps are 6 mm, about ten real grains across, so fine detail like single grains or thin rake lines is drawn rather than simulated. The sand outside a 28 × 12 cm block around the ball is a surface the spray lands on. That block's walls absorb waves, so they don't bounce back as if from a box. Each shot takes 20–40 seconds to work out; a later pass will speed all the labs up.
